excerpt: The injuries rear-end collisions cause most often, why symptoms can take days to appear, and what that delay does to a claim.
keyTakeaways: Rear-end collisions account for 29% of all U.S. crashes and frequently cause whiplash, herniated discs, concussions, and chronic pain that may not appear for days after the accident. The rear driver is typically presumed at fault, and victims can recover compensation for medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, and more. Seeking immediate medical attention is essential for both your health and your injury claim.

faqs.question: What is the most common injury from a rear-end collision?
faqs.answer: Whiplash is the most common injury from a rear-end collision. It occurs when the head is violently thrown backward and then forward upon impact, stretching and tearing the muscles, tendons, and ligaments in the neck. Up to 50% of whiplash victims experience symptoms lasting more than a year.

faqs.question: Can I still recover compensation if my injuries did not appear right away?
faqs.answer: Yes. Delayed symptoms are extremely common after rear-end accidents. Adrenaline and endorphins can mask pain for hours or days. As long as you seek medical attention promptly after the accident and document the connection between the crash and your injuries, you can pursue a claim for delayed-onset injuries.

faqs.question: Who is at fault in a rear-end accident?
faqs.answer: The rear driver is typically presumed to be at fault because all drivers have a legal duty to maintain a safe following distance. However, this presumption is rebuttable — the rear driver may argue that the lead driver contributed to the crash through sudden unexpected braking, non-functioning brake lights, or reversing into the rear vehicle.

faqs.question: Can a low-speed rear-end collision cause serious injuries?
faqs.answer: Yes. Even rear-end crashes at 10 to 15 miles per hour generate enough force to cause whiplash, herniated discs, and concussions. The severity depends on factors like vehicle size differences, headrest position, and whether the occupant was braced for impact. Never assume a low-speed collision is harmless.

faqs.question: What compensation can I recover after a rear-end accident?
faqs.answer: You may recover compensation for past and future medical expenses, lost wages and lost earning capacity, pain and suffering, emotional distress, loss of enjoyment of life, and property damage. In cases involving egregious conduct like drunk driving, punitive damages may also be available.

faqs.question: Should I see a doctor even if I feel fine after being rear-ended?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. Many rear-end collision injuries — including whiplash, concussions, and herniated discs — produce delayed symptoms that may not appear for hours or days. Seeking immediate medical evaluation protects your health and creates documented evidence linking the accident to your injuries, which is critical for any future injury claim.
